title: Sheninagans in Kogi
bodyHtml:
Kogi is a language spoken by around 10,000 people in Colombia. Two Kogi-speaking friends are talking to each other. The picture below shows an illustration of one situation where the phrase akhiengua nigukú might occur in their dialogue.

Below are eight more excerpts of dialogue in Kogi and illustrations of situations in which they might occur, in arbitrary order.

No.ExcerptNo.Excerpt
1akhiengua nagukú5kwisaté nagukú
2akhiengua namagu6kwisaté nigukú
3ga nigukú7mowi nagukú
4ga nimagu8mowi nimagu

assets.alt: Two stick figures in conversation, illustrating the example phrase.
Eight lettered panels A to H showing two stick figures in different conversational situations.
Three further panels numbered 9, 10 and 11 showing two stick figures in conversation.

questions.partPrompt: Match each excerpt of dialogue 1–8 to its corresponding situation A–H.
Here are three more situations, shown in the panel above. Write the Kogi dialogue that would be appropriate for each.

hints.text: Ignore the first word of each excerpt to begin with. Look only at the second word, and sort the eight excerpts into groups by it. Then look at what the pictures in each group have in common.

The second word is built from three pieces, and two of them vary independently. One piece tracks who the subject is — the speaker or the listener. The other tracks something subtler about what the speaker assumes the listener already knows.

Split the second words: na-gu-kú, ni-ma-gu, ni-gu-kú, na-ma-gu. There is a shared root gu. The prefix is na- or ni-, and the remaining piece is either -kú or ma-. Compare akhiengua nagukú with akhiengua namagu: only the subject changes between those two pictures. That tells you what -kú and ma- encode. Now work out na- versus ni- from the remaining pairs.

explanationHtml:
The first word of each excerpt is the root — the thing being said or done. The second word carries all the grammar, and it decomposes into three slots.

Phrase structure

SlotFormMeaning
Prefixna-asymmetric
Prefixni-symmetric
Subjectma-subject is you
Subject-kúsubject is I
Rootgushared across all forms

So the second word is prefix + gu, with the subject marker either preceding (ma-) or following (-kú) the root.

What symmetric and asymmetric mean

These are terms for what linguists call epistemological perspective: the speaker's assumption about what the listener already knows.

  • Asymmetric (na-) — the speaker is telling the listener something they do not expect the listener to already know. New information.
  • Symmetric (ni-) — the speaker is saying something they assume the listener already knows, often for emphasis or rhetorical effect.

This is why the pictures matter so much. A panel where the listener is visibly surprised signals new information; a panel where both figures can already see what is being discussed signals shared knowledge.

Building the answers

For situation 9, the root is ga and the subject is the speaker, with information the listener does not have: ga nagukú. For 10, the root is akhiengua, the subject is the listener, and the information is shared: akhiengua nimagu. For 11, the same symmetric-listener frame with root kwisaté: kwisaté nimagu.

Grammatical marking of who-knows-what is called evidentiality or engagement, and it is obligatory in many languages of South America. English has nothing that forces you to mark it, which is exactly why this problem is hard on a first read.
